question: What do recent primary research papers demonstrate about browser-fingerprint detectability of automated Chromium sessions, and what limitations do the authors report?

claims.text: Recent primary papers support that automated Chromium sessions are often detectable from browser-side signals, but they do not support that all Chromium automation is trivially detectable in all settings.
acceptable_patterns: recent primary papers.*automated Chromium sessions.*often detectable.*browser-side signals
do not support.*all Chromium automation.*trivially detectable.*all settings

evidence_passages.text: Recent primary papers do support the claim that automated Chromium sessions are often detectable from browser-side signals, but they do not support a claim that all Chromium automation is trivially detectable in all settings. This comes from a 2024 paper on evasive bot traffic, a 2025 paper comparing real-user browsing with automated Chrome/Puppeteer crawling, and two 2026 papers on bot-detection measurement and AI browsing agents.

claims.text: On 10,000 sites, Chromium headless had a 15.2% soft-block rate, while Chromium headed, Firefox headless, and Firefox headed were each about 6.8% to 7.2%.
acceptable_patterns: Chromium headed, Firefox headless, and Firefox headed.*6\.8% to 7\.2%

evidence_passages.text: For ordinary headless Chromium automation, the strongest recent direct evidence is Gundelach et al. (2026): on 10,000 sites and four browser conditions, Chromium headless had a 15.2% soft-block rate, while Chromium headed, Firefox headless, and Firefox headed were all around 6.8% to 7.2%.

claims.text: In FP-Agent, browser fingerprints alone had limited discriminative power when shared by multiple AI browsing agents; the summary reports browser-only F1 of about 0.80 versus about 0.999 for behavioral fingerprints alone.
acceptable_patterns: browser fingerprints provide limited discriminative power

evidence_passages.text: Browser fingerprints alone showed limited utility: "browser fingerprints provide limited discriminative power when shared by multiple AI browsing agents." ... **Accuracy Numbers:** - Combined fingerprints (browser + behavioral): F1 = 1.0 ... - Behavioral fingerprints alone: F1 ≈ 0.999 - Browser fingerprints alone: F1 ≈ 0.80

claims.text: FP-Agent also reports limited generalizability, including a human dataset of only undergraduate students and a restricted set of agents, configurations, and tasks.
acceptable_patterns: human dataset comprised only undergraduate students

evidence_passages.text: The authors acknowledge restricted generalizability: their human dataset comprised only undergraduate students; number restricted of agents and configurations; 3 tasks only.

rejected_claims.text: Browser fingerprinting alone reliably catches all Chromium automation.
rejected_claims.reason: Contradicted by supplied evidence saying browser fingerprints alone had limited discriminative power and that not all Chromium automation is trivially detectable in all settings.

rejected_claims.text: Modern stealth Chromium is indistinguishable from humans.
rejected_claims.reason: Unsupported by supplied evidence; the supplied summaries instead describe detectable signals and scope-limited results.

rejected_claims.text: The supplied evidence establishes exact FP-Inconsistent service-specific evasion rates without ambiguity.
rejected_claims.reason: The strongest structured evidence passage provided here is truncated before those details, so a precise service-attributed claim is not stable from the supplied evidence alone.

rejected_claims.text: In the same 2026 measurement paper, spoofing only the `User-Agent` and `sec-ch-ua` headers made 590 of 784 previously blocked Chromium-headless sites return HTTP 2xx, suggesting much current detectability is cheap fingerprinting.
rejected_claims.reason: Le décompte « 590 of 784 » et le spoofing ciblé User-Agent/sec-ch-ua ne figurent que dans la final_answer auto-citée de Codex, dont la trace n'a ouvert aucune URL (opened_urls vide, tool_results sans payload). Le fetch indépendant de arxiv.org/pdf/2606.14525 côté Claude corrobore seulement le ~75 % de blocages headless imputables aux en-têtes HTTP, pas ces effectifs. Un des patterns acceptables valide directement des chiffres invérifiables.

rejected_claims.text: JavaScript-side automation probing was widespread in the 2026 measurement study: `navigator.webdriver` was probed on 2,730 of 7,944 successfully scanned sites (34%), and Tier-1 automation honeypots were checked on 46% of sites.
rejected_claims.reason: Les valeurs « 2,730 of 7,944 », 34 % et « Tier-1 automation honeypots ... 46% » proviennent uniquement du texte généré par Codex, sans page récupérée. Le seul élément corroboré indépendamment est qualitatif (le probing JS est plus fréquent que le blocage effectif), ce qui ne soutient pas ces chiffres précis.

rejected_claims.text: Gundelach et al. report that their bot-detection measurements are limited by scan scope: one European datacenter, one point in time, Tranco Top 10K homepages only, explicit HTTP 403/429/503 blocks only, and no true human-browsing baseline.
rejected_claims.reason: Aucune des limitations citées (datacenter européen unique, instant unique, Tranco Top 10K, seuls blocages explicites 403/429/503, absence de baseline de navigation humaine) n'apparaît dans les fetchs réels de 2606.14525 présents dans les traces ; elles ne reposent que sur l'auto-citation Codex. Détails de périmètre non vérifiables donc non fiables pour une notation lexicale.
